title: Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) from a Psychodynamic Perspective - A Case Report
content: Introduction: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is a condition characterized by the presence of at least two distinct identities. Each identity has unique patterns of perception, of making interactions, of thinking about oneself and one's surroundings. The experience of severe trauma, particularly in childhood, is considered the most common etiological source. Diagnosis of DID is difficult, requiring observation and understanding of complex mechanisms. In this paper, the authors used a holistic approach to the psychiatric and psychological diagnosis process. Case Presentation: A 33-year-old woman presented to the Department of Psychiatry, Medical University of Bialystok, due to frequent amnestic states accompanied by a lack of continuity of autobiographical memory. The patient had previously been treated at the Mental Health Outpatient Clinic with suspected schizophrenia. The patient's history was difficult to collect and switches between identities were observed, with a marked change in behavior. The stories she reported changed, depending on the dominant identity, each of which varied in terms of gender, name, sexual orientation, interests or pattern of behavior. Outcome: The patient underwent a thorough laboratory diagnosis, including toxicologic diagnosis, neuroimaging and psychological diagnosis. On the basis of the information collected, based on the ICD-10 Classification, the diagnosis was: F44.8 - dissociative identity disorder. Discussion: The clinical entity described by the authors still poses many diagnostic and therapeutic uncertainties. In the literature, we do not find a case description that holistically encompasses DID. Therefore, the following description represents a unique bibliographic item, useful to professionals in planning medical and therapeutic care.
